paragraphs: Kiddush, whether by day or by night, must be recited only in the actual place of the meal, as it is said, "and you shall call the Sabbath a delight," and our Sages of blessed memory expounded: the recitation of Kiddush must be where the delight of the Sabbath meal is. Therefore, not only does one who recited Kiddush and did not eat a meal afterward fail to fulfill his obligation, but even one who recited Kiddush in this house and eats in another house — whether his intention from the start was to eat in the other house, or his intention was to eat in the house where he recited Kiddush and he later changed his mind and decided to eat in the other house — he has not fulfilled his obligation, and he must recite Kiddush again before eating in the other house. Some say that if, while eating in the other house, he can see from there the place where he recited Kiddush, even through a window and even only part of it, these two places are considered as one place for the purpose of Kiddush and he need not recite Kiddush again; one should not rely on this reasoning as the primary practice, and should therefore be careful not to bring himself into such a situation. In a time of pressing need, where he was compelled to do so and cannot recite Kiddush in the other house, one may rely on the reasoning of those who are lenient when he can see his place, even from house to house.

clarification.explanation: Kiddush, whether by day or night, must be recited in the place where the Sabbath meal is actually eaten, as it is said, "and you shall call the Sabbath a delight," and the Sages expounded that Kiddush must be recited where the delight of the meal is. Therefore, not only does one who recites Kiddush and does not eat afterward fail to fulfill his obligation, but even one who recites Kiddush in one house and goes to eat in another fails to fulfill it — and it makes no difference whether he planned in advance to eat in the other house or changed his mind afterward. In such a case he must recite Kiddush again before eating. Some say that if, while eating in the other house, he can see from there the place where he recited Kiddush, even through a window and even only part of it, the two places are considered one, and he need not recite Kiddush again. One should not rely on this leniency as the primary practice and should be careful not to get into such a situation; but in a case of great difficulty where there is no choice, one may rely on the lenient opinion that seeing one's place, even from house to house, suffices.
takeaways: Kiddush must be recited where the meal is eaten
If one recited Kiddush in one house and ate in another, he must recite Kiddush again
In a time of pressing need, one may rely on the opinion that seeing the place of Kiddush, even through a window, suffices

paragraphs: Two rooms in one house, and he recited Kiddush in this room and eats in the other room, or he recited Kiddush downstairs and eats upstairs — if this was not his intention and he cannot see his place, he has not fulfilled his obligation. But if this was his intention, even though he cannot see his place, he need not recite Kiddush again, since it is one house; nevertheless, one should not do this as the primary practice. And if he is compelled to eat in the second place, he should be careful to eat an olive's-worth in the place where he recited Kiddush, and only afterward eat in the second place. Here in our city of Baghdad this matter is common among the women, whose way is not to eat at the table with the men even when there are no outside guests, but their way is to hear Kiddush in the dining room from the master of the house, and afterward they go to another room and eat. If they could see the place of Kiddush from that room, even part of it, we would have kept silent; but the difficulty is that the place of Kiddush is not visible at all. This is found mostly in the large houses of the wealthy; therefore they should be careful to eat an olive's-worth in the place of Kiddush and then go to another room to eat there.

clarification.explanation: If there are two rooms in the same house, and he recited Kiddush in one room and wants to eat in the second room, or he recited Kiddush downstairs and wants to eat upstairs — if he did not plan this in advance and cannot see the place of Kiddush, he has not fulfilled his obligation. But if he planned this in advance, even though he cannot see the place of Kiddush, he need not recite Kiddush again, since the two rooms are in the same house. Nevertheless, one should not act this way as the primary practice, and if he is compelled to eat in the second room he should be careful to first eat an olive's-worth of food in the place where he recited Kiddush, and only afterward go to eat in the second room. In Baghdad this is common among women, who are not accustomed to sit and eat with the men but hear Kiddush in the dining room from the master of the house and go to eat in another room. If they can see the place of Kiddush from there, there is no problem, but usually in the large houses they cannot see it, and therefore they should be careful to eat an olive's-worth in the place of Kiddush before going to eat in another room.
takeaways: Two rooms in the same house — if planned in advance, one need not recite Kiddush again, but this should not be done as the primary practice
The practical advice: eat an olive's-worth in the place of Kiddush, then move to another room
This ruling is especially relevant to women who are accustomed to eat in a separate room

paragraphs: Even within one room, if he recited Kiddush in this corner intending to eat there, and changed his mind to eat in a second corner, one should not do this as the primary practice, even though Maran of blessed memory ruled leniently, following the Rambam and the Rosh of blessed memory, that it is permitted; nevertheless the Rif of blessed memory and those who agree with him disagree. And the later authorities of blessed memory wrote that even Maran of blessed memory would agree that as the primary practice one should not act this way; therefore, here too one should act accordingly: eat an olive's-worth first in the corner where he recited Kiddush, and only afterward turn to the other corner.

clarification.explanation: Even within one room, if he recited Kiddush in one corner with the intention of eating there, and afterward changed his mind and wanted to eat in another corner — he should not do so as the primary practice. Although Maran ruled leniently on this, following the opinion of the Rambam and the Rosh, the Rif and his followers disagree, and the later authorities wrote that even Maran would agree that as the primary practice it is not proper to act this way. Therefore here too the correct way is to first eat an olive's-worth in the corner where he recited Kiddush, and only afterward move to the other corner.
takeaways: Even moving from corner to corner within the same room is not proper as the primary practice
Even the lenient opinions agree that as the primary practice one should first eat an olive's-worth in the place of Kiddush

paragraphs: One must eat in the place of Kiddush immediately; and if he did not eat until after some time had passed, he has not fulfilled his obligation. But if his intention was to eat immediately, and he was only prevented by circumstances beyond his control and delayed for some time, he has fulfilled his obligation. However, there are those who disagree even with this and hold that even if his original intention was to eat only after some time, even after an hour or two, and even after the time it takes to digest a meal, he has fulfilled his obligation after the fact. And since we hold that in a case of doubt concerning blessings we are lenient, in every such case he should not recite Kiddush again. However, if this happened at the Kiddush of the night, then before he recites the blessing of "Who brings forth bread," he should have the blessing of Kiddush in mind, or say it with his mouth without mentioning God's name and sovereignty; and if it is by day, he should have the commandment of Kiddush in mind during the blessing of "Who brings forth bread," like one who recites Kiddush over bread, and he should recite the verses of the sanctification of the day before washing his hands.

clarification.explanation: One must eat in the place of Kiddush immediately after reciting it, and if he delayed and did not eat until some time had passed, he has not fulfilled his obligation. But if he intended to eat immediately and was only prevented by circumstances beyond his control that delayed him, he has fulfilled his obligation. There are lenient opinions that hold that even if he planned from the outset to eat only after some time — even an hour or two, and even after the time it takes to digest — he has fulfilled his obligation after the fact. Since there is a rule that we are lenient in cases of doubt concerning blessings, in any such case he should not go back and recite Kiddush again. Nevertheless, if this happened at the Kiddush of the night, before reciting the blessing of "Who brings forth bread" he should have the blessing of Kiddush in mind, or say it quietly without mentioning God's name; and if it is by day, he should have the commandment of Kiddush in mind during the blessing of "Who brings forth bread," as one who recites Kiddush over bread, and recite the verses of the sanctification of the day before washing his hands.
takeaways: One must eat immediately after Kiddush; if he delayed intentionally, he has not fulfilled his obligation
If he was prevented by circumstances beyond his control and delayed, he has fulfilled his obligation
Out of doubt, one does not recite Kiddush again, but should have the blessing in mind

paragraphs:
A person may recite Kiddush for others even though he does not eat with them, and there is no concern of "Kiddush not in the place of a meal," since for the listeners who fulfill their obligation, it is the place of their meal. However, wherever the one reciting Kiddush does not eat — whether because he himself does not thereby fulfill his obligation of Kiddush, or because he has already recited Kiddush for himself in the place of his own meal and is reciting it here only for the sake of others — he should not, as the primary practice, recite Kiddush for others unless they do not know how to recite it themselves.
And if these others for whom he is reciting Kiddush do not know how to recite the blessing of Kiddush, but do know how to recite the blessing of "Who creates the fruit of the vine," Rabbi Ḥesed LeAlafim of blessed memory raised the question of whether he may recite that blessing for them as well; and he wrote that it stands to reason that one person should say the entire Kiddush, and therefore it is better that he drink a quarter-log there. And I wrote, with the help of Heaven, in my holy book Makbetzal: if he has already recited Kiddush at home and eaten, and comes to recite Kiddush for these others, it suffices for him to merely taste the wine; but if he has not yet recited Kiddush, it is forbidden for him to taste this wine, since he is not eating there, as we shall write below. And if he drinks a full quarter-log as Rabbi Ḥesed LeAlafim wrote, this is subject to dispute as we shall explain below; however, we shall explain below that one may rely on the opinion of those who permit drinking a quarter-log in a time of need, and accordingly in our case too this is considered a time of need, and the Rabbi ruled well in instructing him to recite the blessing of "Who creates the fruit of the vine" as well and drink a quarter-log. All this applies when he later goes home to recite Kiddush and eat, and his children and household are there, whom he exempts together with himself by reciting Kiddush; but if in his house there is no other person for him to exempt, and he will recite Kiddush there only for himself, then he again runs into the crux of the dispute, since there are those who hold that if he recited Kiddush elsewhere and drank a quarter-log of wine, he has fulfilled the requirement of "Kiddush in the place of a meal." Therefore, such a person, who will afterward recite Kiddush at home only for himself, should not bring himself into the situation of reciting Kiddush for others first relying on the fact that he will drink a quarter-log there. All this applies to the Kiddush of the night, which has its own blessing of Kiddush; but by day, when there is no blessing of Kiddush, there is no such concern, and he may recite Kiddush for others first, recite the blessing of "Who creates the fruit of the vine," and drink a quarter-log, and afterward go home and recite Kiddush even for himself alone, since he recites only the blessing of "Who creates the fruit of the vine."

clarification.explanation: A person may recite Kiddush on behalf of others in order to exempt them from their obligation even though he himself does not eat with them, and there is no deficiency of "Kiddush not in the place of a meal," since the listeners who are exempted are in the place of their own meal. However, when the one reciting it does not eat there, or has already recited Kiddush for himself in the place of his own meal and is reciting it here only for the sake of others, he should not, as the primary practice, recite it for them unless they do not know how to recite Kiddush themselves. If those others do not know how to recite the blessing of Kiddush but do know how to recite "Who creates the fruit of the vine" themselves, Rabbi Ḥesed LeAlafim raised the question of whether the one reciting Kiddush may recite that blessing for them as well (so that one person says the whole Kiddush), and he wrote that it seems preferable that he say the whole Kiddush himself, and therefore it is better that he drink a quarter-log of the wine there — and this counts for him as "Kiddush in the place of a meal" specifically when he afterward goes home, where his household is, and he exempts them together with himself in reciting Kiddush there. But if there is no one else at home for him to exempt, and he is going to recite Kiddush there only for himself, he again enters into the doubt of the dispute as to whether drinking a quarter-log elsewhere counts as "Kiddush in the place of a meal," and therefore such a person should not bring himself to recite Kiddush for others relying on the fact that he will drink a quarter-log there. All this concerns the Kiddush of the night, which has its own blessing; but by day, when there is no blessing of Kiddush, the matter is easier, and he may recite Kiddush for others first, recite "Who creates the fruit of the vine," and drink a quarter-log, and afterward go home and recite Kiddush even for himself alone.
takeaways: One may recite Kiddush for others even without eating with them, since they are in the place of their own meal
As the primary practice, one should do this only if they do not know how to recite Kiddush themselves
If he later returns home to recite Kiddush for himself alone without household members present, he should not rely on the quarter-log he already drank elsewhere, since this is disputed
The daytime Kiddush is easier, since it has no special blessing of Kiddush

paragraphs: If he recites Kiddush for others and does not eat with them, and he has not yet recited Kiddush at his own home, he should not taste anything at all from the cup, for it is forbidden to taste before Kiddush, since he does not fulfill his obligation with this Kiddush, as Kiddush is valid only in the place of a meal.

clarification.explanation: One who recites Kiddush on behalf of others and does not eat with them, and has not yet recited Kiddush for himself at home, is forbidden to taste anything at all from the cup of wine, since it is forbidden to taste before Kiddush, and he himself does not fulfill his obligation with this Kiddush, as it is not in the place of his own meal.
takeaways: One who recites Kiddush for others not in the place of his own meal should not taste from the cup
The reason: he himself has not fulfilled his obligation with this Kiddush, and it is forbidden to taste before Kiddush

paragraphs: Even though we said that Kiddush is valid only in the place of a meal, nevertheless, if he ate an olive's-worth of bread or an olive's-worth of grain foods, or drank a quarter-log of wine in addition to the cup of Kiddush, he has fulfilled his obligation of Kiddush there, and he may afterward eat elsewhere without reciting Kiddush again; however, other fruits and beverages do not suffice for this. And although some say that it suffices to drink a quarter-log from the cup of Kiddush itself, nevertheless one should not rely on this reasoning except in a time of need, such as the cup used at a circumcision when there is no infant there to give it to. Here in our city of Baghdad, may it be protected, the widespread custom is that the mohel recites the blessing over the cup of the circumcision and drinks a quarter-log from it, even though there are several infants present, and they do not give the infant to drink; therefore the mohel must intend thereby to fulfill his obligation of Kiddush and drink a full quarter-log.

clarification.explanation: Even though we said "there is no Kiddush except in the place of a meal," if he ate, in the place of Kiddush, an olive's-worth of bread or of grain foods, or drank a quarter-log of wine in addition to the cup of Kiddush, he has fulfilled his obligation of Kiddush there, and may afterward eat his meal elsewhere without having to recite Kiddush again. Other fruits and beverages do not suffice for this. Some say it is enough to drink a quarter-log from the cup of Kiddush itself, but one should not rely on this opinion except in a time of need, such as the cup used at a circumcision when there is no infant there to give it to drink. In Baghdad the custom is that the mohel recites the blessing over the cup of the circumcision and drinks a quarter-log from it, and therefore he must intend thereby to fulfill his obligation of Kiddush and drink a full quarter-log.
takeaways: Eating an olive's-worth of bread or grain foods, or drinking an additional quarter-log of wine, fulfills the obligation, and one may then eat elsewhere
Other fruits and beverages do not suffice for this
Drinking a quarter-log from the cup of Kiddush itself suffices only in a time of need

paragraphs: If he heard Kiddush from his neighbor, he has fulfilled his obligation, since the listener hears it in the place of his own meal, and it is only required that the one reciting Kiddush intend to exempt him.

clarification.explanation: One who heard Kiddush from the mouth of his neighbor has fulfilled his obligation, since the listener is in the place of his own meal. The condition for this is that the one reciting Kiddush intend to exempt the listener from his obligation.
takeaways: One can fulfill the obligation by hearing Kiddush from a neighbor
Condition: the listener is in the place of his own meal and the one reciting Kiddush intends to exempt him

paragraphs: Some say that Kiddush may be recited only in a place with a lit candle; and some say that Kiddush does not depend on a candle. One should be careful, as per the first opinion, to recite Kiddush in a place with a candle, for so it is fitting to be according to the esoteric tradition, and only for a great need and necessity may one rely on the second opinion.

clarification.explanation: Some say that Kiddush may be recited only in a place where there is a lit candle, and some say that Kiddush does not depend on a candle. It is fitting to be careful, as per the first opinion, to recite Kiddush in a place with a candle, for so it is proper according to the esoteric tradition, and only for a great need and necessity may one rely on the second opinion.
takeaways: It is fitting to recite Kiddush in a place with a lit candle, so it is proper according to the esoteric tradition
Only in a case of great necessity may one recite Kiddush without a candle

paragraphs: It is a positive commandment from the Torah to sanctify the Sabbath with words, as it is said, "Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it" — remember it with remembrances of Sabbath and sanctification. And one must remember it upon its entrance with Kiddush and upon its departure with Havdalah; and some say that Havdalah is a rabbinic enactment, and that from the Torah one is only required to remember it upon its entrance, and therefore from the Torah a person fulfills his obligation with the evening prayer of the Sabbath, and it was only our Sages of blessed memory who enacted that Kiddush be recited over wine. Nevertheless, some say: whoever has wine does not fulfill the Torah obligation of Kiddush through prayer; and some also say: whoever does not have the intention in his prayer to fulfill the obligation of Kiddush does not fulfill it from the Torah.

clarification.explanation: It is a positive commandment from the Torah to sanctify the Sabbath with words, as it is said, "Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it" — to remember the Sabbath and sanctify it. One must remember it upon its entrance with Kiddush and upon its departure with Havdalah. Some say that Havdalah is a matter of the Sages, and that from the Torah it suffices to remember it upon entrance alone; accordingly, from the Torah a person already fulfills his obligation with the Sabbath evening prayer, and it was the Sages who enacted the recitation of Kiddush over wine. However, some say that one who has wine does not fulfill the Torah obligation of Kiddush through prayer, and some say that one who does not have the intention in his prayer to fulfill the obligation of Kiddush does not fulfill it from the Torah.
takeaways: Kiddush is a positive Torah commandment from the verse "Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it"
The Sages enacted that Kiddush be recited over wine
According to some opinions, one who has wine, or did not have the intention in prayer, does not fulfill the Torah obligation through prayer

paragraphs: Kiddush on a festival is a rabbinic matter, yet it has the law of the Sabbath Kiddush in every respect. Women, too, are obligated in the Sabbath Kiddush from the Torah and in the festival Kiddush by rabbinic law, as it is written, "Remember" and "Observe" — whoever is included in "observe" is included in "remember" (Berakhot 20b).

clarification.explanation: The Kiddush of a festival is a matter of the Sages, yet in every respect it has the law of the Sabbath Kiddush. Women, too, are obligated in Kiddush — in the Sabbath Kiddush from the Torah and in the festival Kiddush by rabbinic law. Although women are generally exempt from time-bound positive commandments, they are obligated in Kiddush, because it is said "Remember" and "Observe," and whoever is commanded regarding the observance of the Sabbath is also commanded regarding its remembrance; and women are commanded regarding observance, and therefore also regarding remembrance.
takeaways: Festival Kiddush is a rabbinic matter, but has the law of any Kiddush
Women are obligated in Sabbath Kiddush from the Torah
The reason: "Remember and Observe" — whoever is included in observance is included in remembrance

paragraphs: A minor, even one who is thirteen years and one day old, if there is doubt whether he has grown two pubic hairs, cannot exempt either a man or a woman from their obligation; and even if the man or the woman had already recited the evening prayer, he does not exempt them, as I wrote, with the help of Heaven, in my holy book Makbetzal; and see Tosefet Shabbat, section 271, subsection 3; Eshel Avraham, beginning of section 271, and Mishb'tzot Zahav there; and Eliyah Rabbah, section 273, subsection 12; see there.

clarification.explanation: A minor, even one who has reached the age of thirteen years and one day, if there is doubt as to whether he has developed the signs of physical maturity (two pubic hairs), cannot exempt either a man or a woman from their obligation, since there is no certainty that he is an adult obligated in the commandments. And even if the man or woman had already recited the evening prayer, the minor does not exempt them from the obligation of Kiddush.
takeaways: A minor about whom there is doubt whether he has developed signs of maturity cannot exempt others from their obligation
This ruling holds even if the listeners had already recited the evening prayer

paragraphs: Even though we hold that Sabbath Kiddush is a Torah matter, it is nevertheless permitted, as the primary practice, to pray and recite Kiddush while it is still day, since we rely, for the halachah, on the opinion that the extension of the Sabbath is a Torah matter. And although the Rambam and those who agree with him disagree, the Magen Avraham, section 267, subsection 3, already brought in the name of the Mordechai that even according to the opinion that the extension of the Sabbath is rabbinic, one fulfills his obligation with this Kiddush, since at the time he recites Kiddush he will afterward come under the Torah obligation. And although the Magen Avraham left this in need of further study, and moreover the Gaon Rabbi Akiva Eiger of blessed memory wrote that from the words of Maran in Kesef Mishneh it is clear that the law is not like the Mordechai — see there — and see further what I wrote, with the help of Heaven, in my holy book Rav Berakhot, page 34, and what I wrote there in the section dealing with the law of redemption — see there; nevertheless, here there is a doubt within a doubt, which likewise tips the scale toward leniency, and therefore the practice in many places has been to recite Kiddush while it is still day, and one who is stringent to recite Kiddush only certainly at night — blessing will come upon him; but one who is stringent to recite Kiddush certainly at night should not pray while it is still day and then wait a long time until certain nightfall to recite Kiddush, since as the primary practice one must recite Kiddush immediately after the prayer, as stated above; rather, he should follow the custom of our teacher the Ari of blessed memory, to receive the Sabbath when the sun is at the tops of the trees, for by the time he finishes the evening prayer, returns from the synagogue, and recites the verses and the liturgical poem and the passage from the Zohar that are customarily recited beforehand, it will be the time of darkness, and he can recite Kiddush.

clarification.explanation: Even though Sabbath Kiddush is a Torah matter, it is permitted as the primary practice to pray the evening prayer and recite Kiddush while it is still day — that is, before nightfall — since we rely on the opinion that the extension of the Sabbath is a Torah matter, and when one accepts the Sabbath upon himself while it is still day, the obligation of Kiddush applies to him. Although there are those who disagree, there is a doubt within a doubt that tips the scale toward leniency, and therefore the practice in many places has been to recite Kiddush while it is still day. One who is stringent to recite Kiddush only at certain nightfall — blessing will come upon him; but if he is stringent in this way he should not pray while it is still day and then wait a long time until night, since as the primary practice one must recite Kiddush immediately after the prayer. Rather, he should follow the custom of the Ari, who received the Sabbath when the sun was at the tops of the trees, so that by the time he finishes the evening prayer, returns from the synagogue, and recites the verses, the liturgical poems, and the passage from the Zohar customarily recited beforehand, it will already be the time of darkness, and he can then recite Kiddush.
takeaways: It is permitted to recite Kiddush while it is still day, based on the law of the extension of the Sabbath
One who is stringent to recite Kiddush only at certain nightfall — blessing will come upon him
One who is stringent should not pray while it is still day, but should follow the Ari's custom of receiving the Sabbath when the sun is at the tops of the trees

paragraphs: A minor who comes of age and becomes thirteen years and one day old on the night of the holy Sabbath — I raised, with the help of Heaven, in my holy book Rav Berakhot, page 34, that he should wait to recite Kiddush until certain nightfall; see there. And it is fitting to rule this way as the primary practice, since there is no trouble or loss in this — what would he lose by waiting until night? And indeed, we certainly rely on the presumption of maturity to be stringent, to say that he has developed two pubic hairs, for it is specifically to be lenient that we do not rely on such a presumption in a matter of Torah law.

clarification.explanation: A minor who comes of age and becomes thirteen years and one day old on the very night of the Sabbath — it is fitting that he wait to recite Kiddush until certain nightfall (the emergence of the stars). This is how it is fitting to rule as the primary practice, since there is no trouble or loss in this — what would he lose by waiting until night? This is because we rely on the presumption to be stringent and say that he has already developed the signs of maturity and is obligated in the commandments from the Torah, and in a matter of Torah law we do not rely on presumption to be lenient.
takeaways: A boy who becomes bar mitzvah on the night of the Sabbath should wait to recite Kiddush until certain nightfall
The reason: there is no trouble or loss in waiting, and in a Torah matter one is stringent

paragraphs: The members of the household who hear Kiddush from the master of the house must pay close attention to hear the blessing of Kiddush from beginning to end. And one whose ears are heavy and cannot hear, or whose master of the house is elderly and stammers, so that they cannot recite Kiddush on their own for several unavoidable reasons — I raised in my holy book Makbetzal that this person who cannot hear the blessing from the master of the house should fix his eyes on the cup in the hand of the master of the house who is reciting Kiddush over it, and recite quietly the entire blessing of Kiddush at the time the master of the house is reciting it. And there I brought the words of the Gaon Rabbi Akiva Eiger of blessed memory in a responsum, section 7, that he instituted a practice of reciting the blessing of Kiddush without an opening and a closing formula, and I raised some question about this — see there. And I relied in this matter on what I wrote based on what Rabbi Birkei Yosef of blessed memory wrote, section 295, letter 4, in the name of Maharai Zin of blessed memory. And in our case this is considered after the fact, since he is unable to recite Kiddush over a cup on his own and hold it in his hand.

clarification.explanation: The members of the household who hear Kiddush from the master of the house must pay close attention to hear the blessing of Kiddush from its beginning to its end. One whose ears are heavy and cannot hear, or whose master of the house is elderly and stammers so that he cannot be heard properly, and who cannot recite Kiddush himself for unavoidable reasons — this person who cannot hear should fix his eyes on the cup in the hand of the master of the house, and recite quietly the entire blessing of Kiddush while the master of the house is reciting it. This situation is considered as after the fact, since he is unable to recite Kiddush over his own cup and hold it in his hand.
takeaways: Listeners must hear the blessing from beginning to end
One who cannot hear should fix his eyes on the cup and recite the blessing quietly along with the one reciting Kiddush
This is a solution after the fact, for one who cannot recite Kiddush himself

paragraphs: A blind person may recite Kiddush and exempt his wife and household from their obligation of Kiddush, since all the halachic authorities disagree with Rabbeinu Yeruḥam's ruling regarding a blind person. However, if there are sighted people at the table, and the blind master of the house does not mind if one of his household recites Kiddush, it is good that this sighted person recite Kiddush, so as to fulfill the obligation according to all opinions, since this is possible.

clarification.explanation: A blind person can recite Kiddush and exempt his wife and household from their obligation, since all the halachic authorities disagree with Rabbeinu Yeruḥam, who was stringent regarding a blind person. Nevertheless, if there are sighted people at the table, and the blind master of the house does not insist that he himself recite Kiddush, it is good that the sighted person recite Kiddush, in order to fulfill the obligation according to all opinions, since this is possible.
takeaways: A blind person recites Kiddush and exempts his household
If there is a sighted person at the table and the master of the house does not insist, it is preferable that the sighted person recite Kiddush to satisfy all opinions

paragraphs: It is forbidden to taste even water before Kiddush, from the time the time of Kiddush arrives, that is, at twilight, even if one has not yet prayed the evening prayer. Nevertheless, one who is fasting is permitted to rinse his mouth before Kiddush. And I raised in my holy book Makbetzal: as long as the sun has not yet disappeared, even from a high wall, this is considered a doubt, and it is forbidden to taste even water. And here in our city of Baghdad, may it be protected, twilight begins seven minutes before the call to the Maghrib prayer, which is called at the end of the twelfth hour; therefore, here in our city, since seven minutes remain until the call to the Maghrib, one should not drink even water, since the obligation of Kiddush has already applied to him, as I wrote in my holy book Rav Pe'alim in a responsum, with the help of Heaven.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to taste anything, even water, before Kiddush, from the moment the time of Kiddush arrives — that is, from twilight — even if one has not yet prayed the evening prayer. One who is fasting is permitted to rinse his mouth with water before Kiddush. As long as sunlight is still visible, even on a high wall, this is considered a doubt, and it is forbidden to taste even water. In Baghdad, twilight begins seven minutes before the call to prayer, which is at the end of the twelfth hour, and therefore once only seven minutes remain until the call, one should not drink even water, since the obligation of Kiddush has already applied to him.
takeaways: From twilight it is forbidden to taste even water before Kiddush
One who is fasting may rinse his mouth
As long as sunlight is still visible, even on a high wall — it is a doubt, and tasting is forbidden

paragraphs: The Kiddush of the night does not depend on the evening prayer, so that if one wishes to accept the Sabbath while it is still day and recite Kiddush and eat and pray the evening prayer at night, he may do so, and it is only required that he begin eating half an hour before the time for reciting the Shema. But the daytime Kiddush depends on the prayer, since as long as one has not prayed the morning prayer, the obligation of Kiddush has not yet applied to him; therefore, on Sabbath morning he may drink water before the prayer, since as he has not yet prayed, the obligation of Kiddush has not applied to him. All this applies to men, upon whom the obligation of the morning prayer applies after dawn; but for women, from the moment dawn rises the obligation of Kiddush applies to them, and they are forbidden to drink water before Kiddush, since some say that women are subject to the Torah law that they have no fixed text and no fixed time for prayer, and by saying some formula of prayer once a day they fulfill their obligation; accordingly, for them, Kiddush does not depend on prayer, and therefore, from the moment dawn rises they are forbidden to taste water before Kiddush, as Rabbi Ḥesed LeAvraham wrote in a responsum, Oraḥ Ḥayim, section 6; see there.

clarification.explanation: The Kiddush of the night does not depend on the evening prayer: one who wishes to accept the Sabbath while it is still day, recite Kiddush, eat, and pray the evening prayer afterward at night, may do so, provided that he begins eating half an hour before the time for reciting the Shema. But the daytime Kiddush does depend on the prayer: as long as one has not prayed the morning prayer, the obligation of Kiddush has not applied to him, and therefore on Sabbath morning he is permitted to drink water before the prayer. All this applies to men, who are obligated in a fixed prayer in the morning. But women — from the moment dawn rises the obligation of Kiddush already applies to them, and they are forbidden to drink water before Kiddush, since some say that women are obligated in prayer from the Torah without a fixed text and without a fixed time, and it suffices for them to say some request once a day, so that for them Kiddush does not depend on prayer at all.
takeaways: The Kiddush of the night does not depend on prayer; the daytime Kiddush depends on the morning prayer
Men are permitted to drink water on Sabbath morning before they have prayed
Women are forbidden to drink water from dawn before Kiddush

paragraphs: If one forgot and ate before Kiddush, even if he ate a full meal, he must recite Kiddush immediately when he remembers, and it is forbidden for him to taste anything from the moment he remembers until he recites Kiddush. And if he was prevented by circumstances beyond his control, or did so deliberately, and did not recite Kiddush at night, he has the opportunity to make it up the entire next day, and he should recite the entire blessing of the night's Kiddush except for the passage of "Vayekhulu," which is not recited by day. And if he also forgot or was prevented by circumstances during the day and did not recite Kiddush, and remembered at the twilight of that day, which is a doubtful time between holy and profane — if he had prayed the Sabbath prayer, whether at night or by day, he has thereby fulfilled the Torah obligation of Kiddush, and only a rabbinic obligation of Kiddush remains upon him; and since it is twilight, which is a doubt between day and night, I raised in my holy book Makbetzal that he should recite Kiddush and say the blessing of the night's Kiddush without mentioning God's name and sovereignty, but rather have God's name and sovereignty in mind in his heart. And I wrote there that one should not say we should not obligate him to recite Kiddush at all, since it is a rabbinic doubt and we hold that in a rabbinic doubt we are lenient — this is not so here, since there are those who hold that whoever has wine does not fulfill the Torah obligation of Kiddush through prayer at all; and moreover, Rabbi Tosefet Shabbat wrote that whoever did not have the intention to fulfill the obligation of Kiddush in his prayer does not fulfill it from the Torah, and therefore he must recite Kiddush over the wine, and recite the blessing of Kiddush without mentioning God's name and sovereignty. And if he did not pray any prayer at all on the Sabbath, then he is obligated in Kiddush from the Torah according to all opinions, and now at twilight he must recite Kiddush over the wine and recite the blessing of Kiddush with God's name and sovereignty, like the law of Grace After Meals, which is a Torah matter, that if one is in doubt about it, he goes back and recites the blessing again.

clarification.explanation: One who forgot and ate before Kiddush, even if he ate a full meal, must recite Kiddush immediately when he remembers, and it is forbidden for him to taste anything from the moment he remembers until he recites Kiddush. One who did not recite Kiddush at night, whether because he was prevented by circumstances or deliberately, may make it up the next day, throughout the entire day, and should recite the entire blessing of the night's Kiddush except for the passage of "Vayekhulu," which is not recited by day. If he also forgot or was prevented during the day and did not recite Kiddush, and remembered at the twilight at the close of the Sabbath, which is a doubtful time between holy and profane — if he had already prayed a Sabbath prayer (at night or by day) and thereby fulfilled the Torah obligation of Kiddush, with only a rabbinic obligation remaining, he should recite Kiddush and say the blessing without mentioning God's name aloud, but rather have God's name in mind in his heart. But if he did not pray any prayer at all on the Sabbath, he is obligated in Kiddush from the Torah, and therefore at twilight he should recite Kiddush over the wine and say the blessing with God's name and sovereignty, like the law of Grace After Meals, which is a Torah matter, where one who is in doubt about it goes back and recites the blessing again.
takeaways: One who forgot and ate before Kiddush should recite it immediately upon remembering
One who did not recite Kiddush at night may make it up the next day, without "Vayekhulu"
One who remembers at the twilight at the close of the Sabbath: it depends whether he had prayed — if so, without God's name and sovereignty; if not, with God's name and sovereignty

paragraphs: There should be a cloth beneath the bread on the table, and a cloth above it, for two reasons: the first, in remembrance of the manna; and the second, so that the Sabbath meal be brought with honor. And there is also a third reason for the upper cloth, because of the shame of the bread.

clarification.explanation: There should be a cloth on the table beneath the bread, and another cloth above it, for several reasons: the first, in remembrance of the manna, which fell in the wilderness surrounded by dew both above and below; the second, so that the Sabbath meal be brought with honor; and there is a third reason for the upper cloth — out of honor for the bread, so that it not be "shamed," so to speak, when the blessing is recited over the wine before it.
takeaways: A cloth is placed beneath the bread and a cloth above it
The reasons: remembrance of the manna, honor of the Sabbath meal, and honor of the bread

paragraphs: The cup of Kiddush, even if it is clean, requires rinsing on the inside and washing on the outside, and must be full to its brim, and must not be blemished, for if one has drunk from it, it has become blemished. It must be whole in its rim and in its base; and a crack, even without any actual missing piece, invalidates it. Another person must hand it to him with both hands, and the one reciting Kiddush should receive it from him with both hands, at his left side opposite his chest, and afterward hold it with his right hand alone, and raise it at least a handbreadth above the table, and fix his eyes upon it so that his mind not wander from it.

clarification.explanation: The cup of Kiddush, even if it is clean, requires rinsing on the inside and on the outside, and must be filled to its brim. It must not be blemished — that is, that people have already drunk from it, since drinking from it blemishes it. The cup must be whole in its rim and its base, and a crack invalidates it even if nothing is actually missing. Another person must hand the cup to the one reciting Kiddush with both hands, and he should receive it with both hands at his left side opposite his chest, and afterward hold it with his right hand alone, raise it at least a handbreadth above the table, and fix his eyes on it so that his mind does not wander from it.
takeaways: The cup requires rinsing inside and out, must be full to the brim, and must not be blemished
It must be whole, without a crack, in its rim and base
The manner of holding it: receive it with both hands, hold it with the right hand, raise it a handbreadth, and fix one's eyes on it

paragraphs: If he has only one cup of wine, he recites Kiddush over it at night, and pours from it into another cup and drinks from that one; for if he drinks from the cup itself, it becomes blemished, and he cannot recite Kiddush over what remains the next day. Therefore he pours some of it into a second cup and drinks from the second cup, and to what remains in the first cup he adds water the next day and recites Kiddush over it. And if only a little remains, such that if he adds water to complete it to a quarter-log there will not remain enough taste of wine for him to recite over it the blessing of "Who creates the fruit of the vine," he should drink all of it at night. All this applies if he has another cup for Havdalah; but if he has no other cup for Havdalah, he should leave this cup for Havdalah, and recite Kiddush at night and by day over bread, since Kiddush can be recited over bread, but Havdalah cannot. See Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 23, and Tosefet Shabbat, subsection 29, and the other later authorities.

clarification.explanation: If he has only one cup of wine, he recites Kiddush over it at night, and before drinking he pours some of it into another cup and drinks from the second one. The reason: if he drinks from the cup itself it becomes blemished, and he will not be able to recite Kiddush over what remains in it the next day; therefore he pours a little into a second cup and drinks from there, and to what remains in the first cup he adds water the next day and recites Kiddush over it. If only a little remains in the cup, such that adding water up to a quarter-log would leave no taste of wine for the blessing of "Who creates the fruit of the vine," he should drink all of it at night. All this applies when he has another cup for Havdalah; but if he has no other cup for Havdalah, he should leave this cup for Havdalah, and recite Kiddush at night and by day over bread, since Kiddush can be recited over bread but Havdalah cannot.
takeaways: A single cup of wine: pour some into another cup and drink from it, saving the rest for the next Kiddush with added water
If too little remains, drink it all at night
If there is no other cup for Havdalah, save the wine for Havdalah and recite Kiddush over bread

paragraphs: As the primary practice, the one reciting Kiddush must taste a full mouthful; and it is the most preferable fulfillment of the commandment to drink a quarter-log. After the fact, if the one reciting Kiddush did not taste it, and one of those at the table tasted a full mouthful, they have all fulfilled their obligation; and it is the most preferable fulfillment of the commandment that they all taste it. Nowadays people are not deterred from drinking from a cup that another has drunk from, out of concern for illness, since it is clear to them that the master of the house who recited Kiddush and drank from the cup is clean and free of illness.

clarification.explanation: As the primary practice, the one reciting Kiddush must taste a full mouthful of the wine (the amount that fills one cheek), and it is the most preferable fulfillment of the commandment to drink a quarter-log. After the fact, if the one reciting Kiddush did not taste it and one of those at the table tasted a full mouthful, they have all fulfilled their obligation, though it is the most preferable fulfillment of the commandment that they all taste it. Nowadays people are not deterred from drinking from a cup that another has drunk from out of concern for illness, since it is clear that the master of the house who recited Kiddush and drank from the cup is clean and free of illness.
takeaways: The one reciting Kiddush tastes a full mouthful, and it is preferable to drink a quarter-log
After the fact, it suffices that one of those at the table tasted a full mouthful
There is no concern about drinking from the shared cup of the master of the house

paragraphs: If he recited Kiddush and, before he tasted it, the cup was spilled, they should bring him another cup, and he should recite the blessing of "Who creates the fruit of the vine" over it, but he should not recite the blessing of Kiddush again, since he has already recited it. The same law applies if he paused with speech that was not for the needs of the meal. And those at the table, too, should be careful not to interrupt with speech before the one reciting Kiddush tastes the wine.

clarification.explanation: If he recited Kiddush and, before he tasted it, the cup spilled, they should bring him another cup and he should recite over it only the blessing of "Who creates the fruit of the vine," but he should not repeat the blessing of Kiddush itself, which he has already recited. The same law applies if he paused with speech unrelated to the needs of the meal between the blessing and the drinking. Those at the table, too, should be careful not to interrupt with speech before the one reciting Kiddush tastes the wine.
takeaways: If the cup spills before tasting, he recites only "Who creates the fruit of the vine" again, not the Kiddush itself
Those at the table should not interrupt with speech until the one reciting Kiddush tastes the wine

paragraphs: One does not recite Kiddush over wine that has a bad odor because it was placed in an unclean vessel, even though its smell and taste are still wine, over which one recites the blessing of "Who creates the fruit of the vine," because of the verse, "Offer it now to your governor, etc." Likewise, one does not recite Kiddush over wine that has been left uncovered; and as the primary practice one should be careful even about a brief period of being uncovered, and only after the fact should one not be strict about it; but if a full night passed while it was uncovered, it becomes invalid for Kiddush even though its smell and taste have not changed.

clarification.explanation: One does not recite Kiddush over wine that has a bad odor because it was placed in an unclean vessel, even though the wine itself has a good smell and taste and one recites the blessing of "Who creates the fruit of the vine" over it; this is because of the verse "Offer it now to your governor" — one should not offer to a commandment something one would not offer to a dignitary. Likewise, one does not recite Kiddush over wine that has been left uncovered (left open). As the primary practice one should be careful even about a brief period of being left uncovered, and after the fact one need not be strict about it; but if a full night passed while it was left uncovered, it becomes invalid for Kiddush even though its smell and taste have not changed.
takeaways: One does not recite Kiddush over wine with a bad odor from an unclean vessel, because of "Offer it now to your governor"
One does not recite Kiddush over wine that has been left uncovered
If a full night passed while it was uncovered, it becomes invalid even if its smell and taste have not changed

paragraphs: Wine that tastes like vinegar, even if it still smells like wine, is not used for Kiddush, and one does not even recite "Who creates the fruit of the vine" over it. But if it tastes like wine, even if it smells like vinegar, one may recite Kiddush over it, since the taste is what determines the matter.

clarification.explanation: Wine that has the taste of vinegar, even if its smell is still that of wine, is not used for Kiddush, and one does not even recite the blessing of "Who creates the fruit of the vine" over it. But if its taste is that of wine, even if its smell is that of vinegar, one may recite Kiddush over it, since the taste is the determining factor.
takeaways: Wine that tastes like vinegar is invalid for Kiddush and even for the blessing over wine, even if it smells like wine
Wine that tastes like wine is valid, even if it smells like vinegar, since taste is the determining factor

paragraphs: Wine made from raisins, which are dried grapes: if moisture would come out of them by pressing before they were soaked in water, it is permitted to soak them in water to extract wine from them and recite Kiddush over it; but if not, it is forbidden to recite Kiddush over this, and one may not even recite the blessing of "Who creates the fruit of the vine" over it.

clarification.explanation: Wine made from raisins (dried grapes): if the raisins would produce moisture by pressing even before they were soaked in water, it is permitted to soak them in water to extract wine from them and recite Kiddush over it. But if the raisins were completely dry and would not produce moisture by pressing, it is forbidden to recite Kiddush over the wine that comes from them, and one does not even recite the blessing of "Who creates the fruit of the vine" over it.
takeaways: Raisin wine is valid only if the raisins would produce moisture by pressing before soaking
Completely dry raisins produce wine that is invalid even for the blessing over wine

paragraphs: If he has no wine at all, he should recite Kiddush over bread. And by night he should do the following: he should wash his hands for the blessing of "Who brings forth bread," sit in his place, and say "Vayekhulu" while the bread is still covered; afterward he should uncover it and recite the blessing of "Who brings forth bread" without yet cutting it, and then recite the blessing of Kiddush while his two hands are still on the bread, and only then cut it and eat. And the reason he must place his hands on the bread during the blessing of Kiddush is: just as he must hold the cup of Kiddush in his hand, so too now, when he recites Kiddush over bread, he must hold the bread in his hand; and it would have been enough for this reason to leave one hand alone on it, but since he must recite the blessing of "Who brings forth bread" with both hands on the bread, it is not proper for him to remove one hand after the blessing of "Who brings forth bread" during the blessing of Kiddush; rather, both his hands should remain until he finishes the blessing of Kiddush and cuts the bread, as mentioned by the later authorities. All this applies at night, when there is a great distinguishing feature for Kiddush through the blessing of Kiddush; but by day, when there is no blessing of Kiddush, there is no distinguishing feature for Kiddush in the blessing of "Who brings forth bread"; therefore, if he has a local intoxicating beverage such as date beer or barley beer or the like, he should wash his hands, take a quarter-log cup of the local beverage, recite the blessing of "By whose word all things came to be," and drink a full mouthful, and only afterward recite the blessing of "Who brings forth bread"; for if he recites the blessing of "Who brings forth bread" first, it is not recognizable that he is reciting Kiddush. And if he has no local intoxicating beverage, or has one but cannot drink it because it would harm him and he is entirely unaccustomed to drinking it at all, he should recite only the blessing of "Who brings forth bread," and cut the bread and eat, but he should first say the verses and the liturgical poem that are customarily recited for the daytime Kiddush.

clarification.explanation: If he has no wine at all, he recites Kiddush over bread. At night he should proceed as follows: wash his hands for the blessing of "Who brings forth bread," sit in his place, and say "Vayekhulu" while the bread is still covered; afterward uncover it and recite "Who brings forth bread" but not yet cut it, and recite the blessing of Kiddush while both his hands are still on the bread, and only then cut it and eat. The reason he places his hands on the bread during the blessing of Kiddush: just as one holds the cup of Kiddush in hand, so too when reciting Kiddush over bread one holds the bread in hand, and since he has already placed both hands on it for the blessing of "Who brings forth bread," it is not proper to remove one hand, but rather both should remain until the end of the Kiddush. All this applies at night, when there is a great distinguishing feature for Kiddush through its special blessing. But by day, when there is no special blessing of Kiddush, if he has an important local beverage such as date beer or barley beer, he should wash his hands, take a quarter-log cup of it, recite the blessing of "By whose word all things came to be" and drink a full mouthful, and only afterward recite "Who brings forth bread" — for if he recites "Who brings forth bread" first, it will not be recognizable that he is reciting Kiddush. And if he has no such local beverage, or has one but cannot drink it because of its harshness, he should recite "Who brings forth bread" alone, and cut the bread and eat, but should first say the customary verses of the daytime Kiddush.
takeaways: No wine — recite Kiddush over bread: say "Vayekhulu," recite "Who brings forth bread," and say the Kiddush with both hands on the bread
By day, Kiddush over a local intoxicating beverage precedes "Who brings forth bread," so that the Kiddush is recognizable
No such beverage, or unable to drink it — recite "Who brings forth bread" alone and say the verses of Kiddush beforehand

paragraphs:
This is the order of Kiddush established according to the words of our teacher the Ari of blessed memory: after the evening prayer he should enter his house, and when he enters the place of the table he should say loudly and with great joy, "Shabbat shalom!" and kiss the hands of his father and mother if they are alive. Afterward he should look at the light of the candles over which the blessing was recited, and look at two candles, intending that one corresponds to "Remember" and one to "Observe." He should also intend that they correspond to the first heh and the last heh of the Name of God. And even though seven candles were lit in honor of the Sabbath, he should look only at two, intending in his looking that the supernal candles shine. Afterward he should stand in the place where he sits at the table and say loudly, "This is the meal of the Holy Field of Apples." Afterward he should circle the table by way of the right, and return to stand in the place where he stood before circling. And then, standing there, he should take in his hand two bundles of myrtle, one corresponding to "Remember" and one to "Observe," and hold them and join them together as they grow, between his two hands, and recite over them the blessing "Fragrant trees," and smell them. And after smelling them, immediately, while they are still joined together between his two hands, he should say, "Remember and Observe were said in a single utterance," and also say this verse: "A sweet savor, an offering by fire to the Lord," for in these words are alluded all the intentions of the blessing over fragrance. Afterward he should return to circle the table a second time in silence while the myrtle is still in his hand; but it is not essential that it be held between both hands while circling — it suffices to hold it in the right hand alone; and if it remains held in both hands, how good and how pleasant, for it is proper to do so. And after he has made the second circling with the myrtle and returned to stand in his original place, the myrtle should remain in his right hand out of affection for the commandment, and he should say, "Peace be upon you, ministering angels, etc.," and should say "King of kings of kings," and not say "From the King, etc.," as mentioned in the prayer book of Rabbi Yaavetz of blessed memory; see Kaf HaChaim. Afterward he should say, "For He will command His angels concerning you, etc.," and intend the Name YHV"Kh, which is formed from the last letters of this verse, and the Name Kal"Kh, which is alluded to in the letter kaf of the word "ki" and the letters "lekh" from the word "malakhav"; and afterward, "The Lord will guard your going out and your coming in, etc." and afterward, without pause, he should immediately say the verses of "A woman of valor, etc.," intending that they are twenty-two verses corresponding to the twenty-two supernal channels which are open and pour forth abundance and blessing from the supernal pool at the source of all the crowns. Afterward he should say "Prepare the meal, etc.," "I will praise the name of the Lord in song, etc.," "The Lord is my strength, etc.," and afterward the liturgical poem "I will sing with praises, etc.," and afterward "May it be Your will, etc.," and afterward the passage from the Zohar, Vayak'hel: "This day is crowned, etc." And know that although our teacher the Ari of blessed memory established the liturgical poem "Azamer, etc.," mentioned above, to be said during the meal, nevertheless the widespread custom in all places is to say it before Kiddush, and so wrote Rabbi Yaavetz of blessed memory; and see the Gaon Chida of blessed memory, section 166, letter 3. And our custom, at times when there is reason to hasten Kiddush, such as during the days of the Omer and the like, is to say the aforementioned liturgical poem during the meal.
Afterward he begins the order of Kiddush, which consists of the preparation of action and the preparation of speech. And before arranging the Kiddush he should say this formula: "For the sake of the union," etc., "Behold we come to fulfill the positive Torah commandment to sanctify the Sabbath and to fulfill the rabbinic positive commandment to sanctify it over wine, as our Sages of blessed memory expounded on the verse 'Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it' — remember it with words said over wine, to repair the root of this commandment in the supernal place. And behold, we are prepared to draw down supernal lights to the Holy Field of Apples through preparation in the secret of action and preparation in the secret of speech. And may it be Your will, O Lord our God and God of our fathers, that it rise before You as if we had intended all the intentions fitting to be intended in the secret of action and the secret of speech which Your servants, the sages of Israel, established for us in the order of the Sabbath Kiddush, and may this Kiddush rise before You together with the Kiddushim of Your children who know and intend properly, and may abundant blessing and sustenance be drawn down into all the holy worlds, and from there may abundant sustenance be drawn to our soul, spirit, and higher soul, to serve You in truth and to keep all Your holy Sabbaths all the days of our lives, in thought, speech, and deed, in awe and love and great joy; and behold we are prepared to accept upon ourselves the positive commandment of repentance, as it is written, 'And you shall return to the Lord your God and hearken to His voice.' And may the pleasantness of the Lord our God be upon us, etc."
And may it be Your will, O Lord our God and God of our fathers, that this be now a time of favor before You, and that there be drawn to us and to our souls and to our sons and daughters and to all Israel abundant peace, goodness and blessing, life, grace, kindness, and mercy, through the twenty-two supernal channels which are open and pour forth abundance and blessing from the supernal pool at the source of all the crowns. And may it be Your will, O Lord, Lord, God of our fathers, that in the merit of the commandment of diluting the cup of Kiddush wine with water, [we may be filled] with Your blessings and with the riches of the gifts of Your hands, and in the merit of Jacob Your perfect one, who sweetened the powers of judgment with kindness, as it is written, "And he brought him wine and he drank" — that he mixed water into the wine for her — so, in Your mercy and Your kindness, may all the powers of judgment and strict justice be sweetened, and may You deal with us in good kindnesses.
And may it be Your will, O Lord our God and God of our fathers, that in the merit of the commandment of the blessing of the Sabbath Kiddush over a full cup of wine, the letters of the word "kos" (cup) — which are kaf, vav, samekh, whose numerical value equals that of the word "the blessing" — be filled, and may they be channels to receive for us the abundance of blessing from the supernal pool, the source of blessings, and may there be fulfilled in us the verse that is written, "The Lord will command the blessing upon you in your storehouses and in all that you put your hand to." And now, O Lord God, be pleased to bless the house of Your servants, and from Your blessing may the house of Your servants be blessed forever. May they be favorable, etc.
Afterward he should begin the preparation of action, which is as follows: while still standing in his place, he should receive the cup with both hands from another person, who should also hold it with both hands and hand it to him, and he should hold the cup with both hands opposite his chest, and afterward remove his left hand and hold it with his right hand alone, in order to include the left within the right. And in the order of this action there are deep intentions and supernal secrets, and therefore you should not omit even a small detail of this order, and should intend, in all of it, that there is a secret in the matter. And after he holds it with the right hand alone, he should then dilute it to sweeten it with water; and it is good that the person who handed him the cup with both hands be the one who performs the dilution with his right hand. And the dilution should be done three times, that is, in three separate pourings, one after another, and he should not pour all the diluting water at once. This matter, that the dilution should be in three pourings, is not mentioned in the words of our teacher the Ari of blessed memory, and is found stated explicitly only in the book Ma'avar Yabok, which did not explain the reason for the matter. And in my holy book Makbetzal I explained, with the help of Heaven, the reason: for it is explained in the words of our teacher the Ari of blessed memory that one should dilute the wine to sweeten it with water that corresponds to the three Names Yud-Heh of the letters heh-heh-yud, whose numerical value equals nine yuds of the expansions Ayin-Bet, Samekh-Gimel, Mem-Heh; and so it is written in the prayer book of our teacher the Rashash of blessed memory. Thus it is found that the secret of the water with which he dilutes the wine is these three times, Yud-Heh mentioned above. And it is found accordingly that a great man said a thing that stands to reason, and certainly this was a tradition he received from reliable kabbalists. Therefore, every person should be careful about this, and blessing of goodness will come upon him. And after the dilution, he should fix his eyes on the cup of wine and look at it, and there is a deep secret and a great intention in this looking. And every ordinary person, it suffices for him to intend, in looking with his right eye, the five Names of YHVH whose numerical value equals "eye," and in looking with his left eye, likewise the five Names of YHVH whose numerical value equals "eye," like this:

clarification.explanation:
This is the order of Kiddush established according to the Ari: after the evening prayer, upon entering his house, he says loudly and joyfully "Shabbat shalom," and kisses the hands of his father and mother if they are alive. Afterward he looks at the light of the candles, focusing on two of them corresponding to "Remember" and "Observe" and to the two letters heh in the Name of God; although seven candles were lit, he looks only at two. Afterward he says "This is the meal of the Holy Field of Apples," circles the table to the right, and returns to his place. He then takes two bundles of myrtle corresponding to "Remember" and "Observe," recites over them the blessing "Fragrant trees," and smells them, saying "Remember and Observe were said in a single utterance" and "A sweet savor, an offering by fire to the Lord." Afterward he circles the table again in silence with the myrtle in hand. Upon returning he says "Peace be upon you," the verse "For He will command His angels concerning you" — intending the holy Names alluded to in its letters — and "The Lord will guard your going out," and then, without pause, "A woman of valor" (twenty-two verses corresponding to the twenty-two supernal channels). Afterward he says "Prepare the meal," "I will praise the name of the Lord," "The Lord is my strength," the liturgical poem "I will sing with praises," "May it be Your will," and finally a passage from the Zohar, Vayak'hel. Although the Ari established the poem "Azamer" to be said during the meal, the widespread custom everywhere is to say it before Kiddush; only at times when there is reason to hasten Kiddush, such as the days of the Omer, is it said during the meal.
Afterward he begins the order of Kiddush itself, which is the preparation of action and the preparation of speech, first saying the formula "For the sake of the union" and requests for the drawing down of abundance and blessing through the twenty-two supernal channels, intending that in the merit of the commandment of diluting the wine of the Kiddush cup with water, the powers of judgment will be sweetened with kindness, just as our father Jacob sweetened judgment ("And he brought him wine and he drank" — that he mixed water into the wine), and that in the merit of the blessing of Kiddush over a full cup of wine, the letters of the word "kos" (cup — kaf, vav, samekh) will be filled, which equal in number "the blessing."
In the preparation of action, he receives the cup with both hands from another person, holds it opposite his chest, holds it with the right hand alone, and dilutes it with water — as explained by Rabbi Yosef Chaim in his book Makbetzal — in three separate pourings, corresponding to the three Names of God in the vocalization Yud-Heh of the letters "heh-heh" [i.e., heh, heh, yud], which equal in number nine yuds of the Names Ayin-Bet, Samekh-Gimel, and Mem-Heh. After the dilution he looks at the cup of wine, and there is a deep secret and great intention in this looking — that he should intend, with his right eye, the five Names of YHVH that equal the numerical value of "eye," and likewise with his left eye, five more Names of YHVH.
takeaways: The Ari's order for welcoming the Sabbath: "Shabbat shalom," looking at the candles, circling the table, the blessing over the myrtle, and the kabbalistic liturgical poems

paragraphs:
It is our custom to also look at one's forehead reflected in the wine, intending that "forehead" is numerically equivalent to "success." And with this the preparation of action is completed, and the repair is made and the light is drawn down to become the sovereignty of the Holy Field of Apples, which is the secret of the last heh of the Name of God, through this preparation of action.
And now remains the second preparation, which is the preparation of speech. For the drawing down of the lights and the repair made in the secret of Kiddush to the aspect of the last heh, called the "Holy Field of Apples," is accomplished through two preparations, which are: one in the secret of action, and the second in the secret of speech, for only through these two preparations specifically is completed the drawing down of the lights and the repair that we need to draw down now, on the night of the Sabbath, in the Kiddush of this meal called "the meal of the Holy Field of Apples."
And this is the matter of the second preparation, that of speech, which is accomplished through the saying of "Vayekhulu" and the blessing of Kiddush, which is the aspect of speech. And first of all one should say the entire psalm, "A psalm of David: the Lord is my shepherd, etc.," and afterward say, "The sixth day, and the heavens were finished." And there are several reasons, according to the esoteric tradition, for why the two words "the sixth day" are added to "Vayekhulu." Afterward he should say, "Attend, gentlemen," and even though he is reciting Kiddush alone with no one else standing with him, he must still say "Attend, gentlemen," for there is a secret and an intention in this. Afterward he should say the blessing of "Who creates the fruit of the vine," and afterward the text of the blessing of Kiddush, which has exactly thirty-five words, and afterward he should sit and drink the cup of wine while seated. And know that at night the entire order of Kiddush and the blessings must be done standing, according to the esoteric tradition; but as for what was said about the drinking of the wine being done seated — even though our teacher Rabbi Chaim Vital of blessed memory so testified regarding the custom of our teacher the Ari of blessed memory, that he would sit and drink it, as mentioned in the book Pri Etz Chaim — there is no strictness in this according to the esoteric tradition; rather, this is a matter of the etiquette of the meal. See Eliyah Rabbah, section 170, subsection 23, quoting in the name of the Rokeach; see there. And see the Talmud, tractate Gittin, page 70a: three things harm a person's body, and one of them is drinking while standing; but the Rambam, in the laws of De'ot, chapter 4, did not mention this, and perhaps he holds that this is only harmful if one does all of these things together at once. And perhaps the reason people are not careful about drinking while standing is for this reason; nevertheless, since we have seen the testimony of Rabbi Chaim Vital regarding the custom of our teacher the Ari of blessed memory in this matter, we must be careful about it.

clarification.explanation: In our custom one also looks at the reflection of one's forehead in the wine, intending that "forehead" is numerically equivalent to "success." With this the preparation of action is completed. Afterward comes the preparation of speech: first he says the entire psalm "A psalm of David: the Lord is my shepherd," then "The sixth day, and the heavens were finished" (adding "the sixth day" for reasons of the esoteric tradition), then "Attend, gentlemen" — which even one reciting Kiddush alone still says, since there is an intention in this — then the blessing of "Who creates the fruit of the vine," and then the text of the Kiddush blessing itself, which has exactly thirty-five words. Afterward he sits and drinks the wine while seated. It should be known that the entire order of Kiddush and the blessings at night must be performed standing, according to the esoteric tradition, but the drinking of the wine is done seated — not for a reason of the esoteric tradition, but as a matter of proper table etiquette, and because of three things that are harmful to the body, among them drinking while standing. Since Rabbi Chaim Vital testified to this custom of the Ari, one must be careful about it.

paragraphs:
In the formula of "Prepare the meal" recited at the meal of the night, one should not conclude with "and the Holy Ancient One and the Small Face come to feast with it." The same law applies to the meals of the morning and the afternoon as well — one should not say this conclusion, even though it is written this way in all the prayer books, and so it is written in the Sefer HaKavanot arranged by Maharashvo of blessed memory. Nevertheless, in the prayer book of our teacher the Rashash of blessed memory and the prayer book of Rabbi Yaavetz, this conclusion is not mentioned. And the honorable Rabbi Rabbi Avraham Mani, may his light shine, wrote to me that perhaps they hold that what is mentioned in the Sefer HaKavanot came from the copyist, and therefore he does not say this conclusion. And I myself act this way and so instruct the public, since there is a great principle applicable everywhere: it is preferable to sit and refrain from acting.
Also regarding the circling of the table, the aforementioned Rabbi, may his light shine, wrote to me that his custom is — even when myrtle cannot be found — to perform the two circlings without myrtle, and I agreed with him on this, since the second circling without myrtle, if it does not help, does not harm, since one circles in silence.

clarification.explanation: In the formula of "Prepare the meal" said at the night meal, one should not conclude with "and the Holy Ancient One and the Small Face come to feast with it," and likewise at the meals of the morning and the afternoon this conclusion should not be said. Although it is written this way in all the prayer books and in the Sefer HaKavanot, it does not appear in the prayer books of the Rashash and of Rabbi Yaavetz, and some have written that this conclusion in the Sefer HaKavanot is perhaps an addition of the copyist. Rabbi Yosef Chaim's own practice, and what he instructs the public, is not to say this conclusion, based on the principle that it is preferable to sit and refrain from acting. Likewise regarding the circlings of the table: even if myrtle cannot be found, one should still perform two circlings without myrtle, since the second circling without myrtle, even if it does not help, does no harm, as it is done in silence.

The principle: it is preferable to sit and refrain from acting
If there is no myrtle, one still performs two circlings of the table without it, since it does no harm

paragraphs: If a festival falls on the Sabbath, our teacher the Ari of blessed memory did not explain how one should act regarding the order of Kiddush and the table; only in the prayer book of our teacher the Rashash of blessed memory, regarding Passover falling on the Sabbath, is it written that one should prepare twelve loaves on the table, and other matters are not explicitly mentioned. Our custom in our house, when a festival falls on the Sabbath, is to circle the table twice and smell the myrtle as on other Sabbaths, and to say "Peace be upon you" and "A woman of valor" and "May it be Your will," and to arrange twelve loaves as on other Sabbaths. We also say "Prepare the meal" and "I will sing with praises," since we find that there is an obligation, according to the esoteric tradition, regarding the three meals; and likewise at the afternoon service we recite the verses "And as for me, may my prayer, etc." Only if the first day of Passover falls on the Sabbath is it not our custom to say the liturgical poem "I will sing with praises," but we do perform the circlings and the myrtle. And I have no sufficient reason to distinguish between the night of Passover and the other nights of festivals regarding this liturgical poem. Likewise, if the festival of Rosh Hashanah falls on the Sabbath, it is not our custom to say the liturgical poem "I will sing with praises," but we do perform the circlings and the myrtle, and may God, blessed be He, enlighten our eyes with His Torah, Amen, so may it be His will.
